What happened in the Nanjing massacre?

The Nanjing Massacre, also called the Rape of Nanjing, was a large-scale atrocity committed by the Imperial Japanese Army after it captured the Chinese capital of Nanjing on December 13, 1937, during the Second Sino-Japanese War.

Over roughly six weeks, Japanese soldiers murdered large numbers of Chinese civilians and disarmed prisoners of war, carried out widespread sexual violence, and engaged in looting and arson. Victims included men, women, and children; many prisoners were executed rather than treated as prisoners of war.

The exact death toll is disputed because wartime records were incomplete and estimates use different geographic areas and time periods. Scholarly estimates commonly range from well over 100,000 to more than 300,000 deaths; China officially commemorates 300,000 victims. The events were documented by Chinese survivors, foreign residents in the Nanjing Safety Zone, journalists, photographs, and later war-crimes trials.

The massacre is widely recognized by historians as one of the worst war crimes of the Second World War, though it remains a politically sensitive issue in East Asian historical memory.

What happened in the Nanjing massacre?

The Nanjing Massacre, also called the Rape of Nanking, was a mass atrocity committed by the Imperial Japanese Army after it captured Nanjing, then China’s capital, on December 13, 1937, during the Second Sino-Japanese War.

Over the following weeks—commonly dated as about six weeks—Japanese troops killed large numbers of Chinese civilians and disarmed soldiers or prisoners of war. They also carried out widespread rape, torture, looting, and arson. Many victims were executed in mass shootings or killed with bayonets and other weapons; women and girls were subjected to systematic sexual violence.

The exact death toll remains debated because of differing boundaries, time periods, and source methods. Major historical estimates commonly range from well over 100,000 to more than 300,000 deaths. The International Military Tribunal for the Far East concluded that at least 200,000 people were killed, while Chinese official commemoration often cites 300,000.

The massacre is extensively documented through survivor testimony, burial records, photographs, diaries, reports by foreign residents and aid workers in the Nanjing Safety Zone, and Japanese military-related evidence. It remains a deeply sensitive issue in China-Japan relations, in part because some Japanese nationalists have minimized or denied its scale despite the broad consensus among historians that mass atrocities occurred.
